APX-000001.transcript:
Customer (David Bell): My bill jumped and I don't understand why. Did something change with my rate?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Hi David Bell, Naledi Nkosi here — let me pull that up.
Customer (David Bell): I've been on the same rate for years, why is this changing now?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Good question, a lot of customers are asking about this one. Let me check your account.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (David Bell): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (David Bell): Is this the Phase 2 thing the AUC approved, or did I do something wrong on my account?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Roughly how much gas do you use in a year, or should I look it up?
Customer (David Bell): No idea. Can you look it up?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Did you get the letter by mail or by email?
Customer (David Bell): By mail, a couple of weeks ago.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Do you have any irrigation or shop meters on the same account?
Customer (David Bell): No, just the house.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Let me take a look. I've pulled up the account, confirmed the Rate 1/Rate 2 threshold under the August 1 Phase 2 restructuring, and walked through what changed on this specific account.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Alright, I can see exactly what's going on here.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Since August 1, Rate 1 covers accounts using under 4,000 GJ a year and Rate 2 covers larger users. The AUC approved it as Phase 2 of the rate restructuring.
Customer (David Bell): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): You're on Rate 1 since your annual usage is under 4,000 GJ, so the main change is the way the distribution charge is broken out on the bill — your total shouldn't move much. I've sent the AUC decision summary to your email so you have it on file.
Customer (David Bell): So my total won't go up much?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): It shouldn't. Most of this month's jump is colder weather, not the rate change.
Customer (David Bell): Can I get that in writing?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): The AUC summary and your usage figure are in your email now.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): To recap: you're staying on Rate 1, the change is mostly how the bill is laid out, and the summary is in your email.
Customer (David Bell): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Customer (Kevin Grant): I signed up for budget billing so my payments would be predictable, and now I've got a CA$600 catch-up bill.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Hi Kevin Grant, Vusi Molefe here — let me pull that up.

Agent (Vusi Molefe): Alright, I can see exactly what's going on here.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): The plan averages your last twelve months of usage and is reviewed at month six. If usage runs higher than the estimate, the difference is added.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): The plan recalculates twice a year against your rolling usage average, and this adjustment reflects higher usage than last year's estimate — I've set up an email alert so you'll get advance notice before the next recalculation instead of finding out on the bill.
Customer (Kevin Grant): Will it change again without warning?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): The next review is in six months, and you'll get an email two weeks before it.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): To recap: the catch-up is spread over the rest of the plan year, and you'll get an email two weeks before the next review.
Customer (Kevin Grant): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Customer (Ryan Campbell): You charged me far more in fees than the gas actually cost. That can't be right.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Hi Ryan Campbell, Kagiso Radebe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Ryan Campbell): Can you actually break down where every line item on this bill comes from?
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Thanks for bearing with us on this. Let me go through the bill with you properly.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Ryan Campbell): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Ryan Campbell): This isn't the first time — I feel like I'm being charged fees just for having an account.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Is the property occupied at the moment?
Customer (Ryan Campbell): It's vacant while we sell it, so the gas is barely on.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Have you raised this with us before?
Customer (Ryan Campbell): Once before, and I was told it's just how the bill works.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Would a line-by-line breakdown by email help?
Customer (Ryan Campbell): Yes, I want to see where every dollar comes from.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Let me take a look. I've reviewed the itemized charges line by line against metered usage and the current distribution rate schedule.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Okay, I've got it pulled up now.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): The distribution charge and the fixed daily charge are set by the AUC for your rate class, so they apply even when the meter reads zero.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): I've gone through every line — the distribution charge and fixed monthly charge apply regardless of usage under your rate class, and I've corrected the one line item that was billed in error. You'll see the adjustment on your next statement.
Customer (Ryan Campbell): So one of them was actually wrong?
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Yes, a late-payment charge was applied after your payment had already cleared. That's the adjustment.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): To recap: the late-payment charge comes off on your next statement, and the line-by-line breakdown is in your email.
Customer (Ryan Campbell): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Customer (Brian Kerr): My estimated bill was way higher than what I actually used last month.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Hi Brian Kerr, Karabo Zulu here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Brian Kerr): If the estimate is wrong, how does the correction actually happen on a future bill?
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Understood. Let me pull up the account and look at the charges before I say anything.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Brian Kerr): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Brian Kerr): Is there a way I can submit my own meter reading instead of waiting?
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Can you see the meter from outside, or is it behind a gate?
Customer (Brian Kerr): It's behind the back gate, and the dog's out there during the day.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Do you have a reading from the meter today?
Customer (Brian Kerr): I took a photo this morning. It's much lower than the bill.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Would a self-read reminder by email work for you?
Customer (Brian Kerr): Yes, if it actually gets used.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Let me take a look. I've checked the meter-read schedule for the account and confirmed whether a self-read or field read was available.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Alright, I can see exactly what's going on here.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): When our reader can't reach the meter, the bill is estimated from your past usage for the same months.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): I've scheduled an actual field read for your next cycle and shown you how to submit a self-read online in the meantime, so this month's estimate will be corrected against the real number once it's read.
Customer (Brian Kerr): So I'll get the overcharge back?
Agent (Karabo Zulu): It's credited automatically on the next bill once the actual read is in.
Customer (Brian Kerr): And the gate?
Agent (Karabo Zulu): I've added an access note so the reader calls ahead.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): To recap: your self-read is on file, the next bill corrects the estimate, and the reader will call ahead about the gate.
Customer (Brian Kerr): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Customer (Robert Scott): I'm following up again — this bill says 'estimated read' again. Can someone come and read my meter?
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Hi Robert Scott, Sipho Nkosi here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Robert Scott): I already explained this on my last contact.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): I'm sorry about that — let me look at what happened last time and pick up from there.

Customer (Robert Scott): Yes, same address as always, and the account's under my name.
Customer (Robert Scott): If the estimate is wrong, how does the correction actually happen on a future bill?
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Do you have a reading from the meter today?
Customer (Robert Scott): I took a photo this morning. It's much lower than the bill.

Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Let me take a look. I've checked the meter-read schedule for the account and confirmed whether a self-read or field read was available.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Thanks for holding — I've got the full picture now.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): When our reader can't reach the meter, the bill is estimated from your past usage for the same months.
Customer (Robert Scott): So is this actually getting fixed today?
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Your meter is on the standard bi-monthly read cycle, so this cycle is estimated by design — I've noted your account for a field read next cycle, but I can't move today's estimate to an actual reading.
Customer (Robert Scott): So this month's estimate just stands?
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): For this cycle, yes. It corrects itself once there's an actual read.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): To recap: this estimate stands for now, a field read is booked for next cycle, and any difference is corrected on that bill.
Customer (Robert Scott): That's not really the answer I was hoping for, but okay.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): I've logged everything here so if this comes up again, the next agent has the full picture.

Agent (Kagiso Radebe): One administration fee was applied twice in July. That's the credit you'll see.
Customer (Chris Bell): And the rest of the fees?
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): They're the regulated distribution and fixed charges. I've emailed you a one-page breakdown of each line.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): To recap: the duplicate fee is credited on this statement, the breakdown is in your email, and the account is flagged so the credit shows before your next bill.
